extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, marketing/communications teams, PR agencies, and corporate communications staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating Video News Releases (VNRs) — short video segments made by PR/marketing teams to be distributed to television newsrooms. Covers structural elements, production dos and don'ts, distribution considerations, and common criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designed to resemble a real news report
rubrics_metrics.description: A video news release is a segment of video that is designed to resemble a real news report; however, instead of being created by a news agency, it is made by a public relations specialist, an advertising agency, or a corporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The segment should look like a news item (format, pacing, reporter presence) so it is usable by newsrooms and can shape public opinion or promote products/services. Note: it is produced by marketers/PR rather than independent news agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide ready-made broadcast content
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea behind a video news release is to provide the media with content that has been ready-made for broadcasting and puts your business, your product, or the services you offer in a positive light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the content immediately usable by stations (broadcast-quality audio/visual, concise storytelling) so journalists can air it in entirety, use portions, or incorporate it into a story at their discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a professional on-air reporter or actor
rubrics_metrics.description: A good VNR will contain a professional news reporter, someone who has on-air experience with the news, or an actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an on-air professional (or convincing actor) to give the segment a credible, polished news-style presentation appropriate for television newsroom use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include interviews with experts with legitimate expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews with experts who usually have legitimate expertise in a topic, though that expertise may be biased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature experts to highlight authority and increase credibility, but be aware and manage potential perceived bias (disclosure, balanced sourcing where possible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use eye-catching visual elements (e.g., company logo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eye-catching visual elements, such as a company’s logo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate strong visuals to draw attention and support the story, but ensure visuals are appropriate and relevant to the content (see 'avoid inappropriate visuals').

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate the products or services being discussed
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations of the products or services that are being discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show practical demonstrations or footage of the product/service in use to illustrate claims and help viewers (and journalists) understand the offering quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a short runtime (typically no longer than 2 minutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A short run time; typically no longer than 2 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the VNR concise so it is easy for newsrooms to slot into broadcasts and for viewers to absorb the key message quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid appearing highly promotional
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly promotional. Though the goal of a VNR is to promote a company, a product, a service, or a person, it shouldn’t appear too promotional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone down overt advertising language and hard-sell techniques; if it appears too promotional it will be viewed as an advertisement rather than news and may be rejected by journalists or criticized as deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive producing
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive producing. Some producing is fine, but too much can detract from the value of a VNR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t overproduce visual/style elements — overly produced pieces limit a newsroom’s ability to add their own spin or integrate the footage naturally into reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate visuals
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure images match the content shared; inappropriate or mismatched visuals undermine credibility and reduce the likelihood of newsroom use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accompanying documentation for newsrooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a news agency receives a video news release, they give it a once over and read any accompanying documentation that may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear written materials (b-roll descriptions, interviewee IDs, key facts, contact info, suggested soundbites) so newsrooms can quickly assess and use the VNR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design segments to be usable whole or in parts by newsrooms
rubrics_metrics.description: News agencies might air a VNR in its entirety, they may air only a portion of it, or they may incorporate it into a news report if it contains information that ties into a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure content so individual clips or soundbites can stand alone and be integrated into broader reporting — this increases the chances of pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent to avoid deceptive 'fake news' perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics have referred to video news releases as deceptive propaganda that tries to influence viewers under the disguise of real news. This is particularly true when it is not made clear that a VNR isn’t real news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider disclosure or clear sourcing to avoid accusations of deception; balance promotional aims with ethical transparency to protect credibility and trust.
